name: Trans-Pacific Route
genZNote: This is the route your phone probably took to get to you — East Asia's factories to North America's ports, container ship after container ship.

sections.heading: 🛳️ Route Path
bullets: East Asian ports (Shanghai, Shenzhen, Busan, Yokohama) → across the open Pacific Ocean → North American west-coast ports (Los Angeles/Long Beach, Vancouver, Seattle).
A more southerly extension continues to Latin American Pacific ports.

sections.heading: 📦 Why It Matters
bullets: One of the highest-volume trade lanes in the world, carrying electronics, machinery, apparel, and consumer goods from East Asian manufacturing hubs to North American markets.
Los Angeles/Long Beach together form one of the busiest port complexes in the world largely because of this route.
Doesn't rely on any single strait or canal chokepoint the way the Suez or Gulf routes do — its main constraint is simply the sheer distance and time of an open-ocean crossing.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: The Trans-Pacific route connects East Asian manufacturing ports to North America's Pacific coast, one of the highest-volume trade lanes in the world.
keyFacts: Path: East Asia → open Pacific Ocean → North America's west coast.
Los Angeles/Long Beach is a key destination port complex.
No single chokepoint — main constraint is open-ocean distance.
commonConfusion: Unlike the Suez or Gulf routes, this one has no strait/canal bottleneck to name — its defining feature is scale, not a chokepoint.

highYieldFacts: Trans-Pacific route: East Asia ↔ North America's west coast.
One of the world's highest-volume container trade lanes.
No major strait/canal chokepoint along it.
commonTraps: Don't try to assign a chokepoint to this route — that's the point of contrast with Suez/Gulf/Malacca routes.
mustRemember: Trans-Pacific route = East Asia-North America's biggest, chokepoint-free trade lane.
